title: Decoupling of Internal and External Workload During a Marathon: An Analysis of Durability in 82,303 Recreational Runners
authors: Smyth B, Maunder E, Meyler S, Hunter B, Muniz-Pumares D
population: Marathon runners with heart-rate and pace data (13,125 female)
findings: Decoupling magnitude (35-40 km segment relative to 5-10 km segment, %HRmax per speed relative to CS) averaged 1.16 +/- 0.22, first detected 25.2 +/- 9.9 km into the marathon; onset was defined as decoupling exceeding 1.025.

Low-decoupling runners (<1.1; 34.5%) ran 88 +/- 6% CS, finished in 217.3 +/- 33.1 min and decoupled at 33.4 +/- 9.0 km; high-decoupling runners (>=1.2; 32.8%) ran 82 +/- 7% CS, finished in 238.5 +/- 30.7 min and decoupled at 19.1 +/- 6.8 km (moderate group: 86% CS, 224.9 min, 22.6 km).
Males had greater decoupling than females (1.17 +/- 0.22 vs 1.12 +/- 0.16) and earlier onset (25.0 vs 26.3 km).
Adding decoupling magnitude and onset to models using CS and the curvature constant reduced marathon prediction error from 6.45% to 5.16%.

Internal workload was %HRmax and external workload was speed relative to estimated critical speed (CS); decoupling magnitude was the 35-40 km segment relative to the 5-10 km segment, with onset defined as the point decoupling exceeded 1.025.
Overall decoupling was 1.16 +/- 0.22, first detected 25.2 +/- 9.9 km into the marathon.

Low decoupling (<1.1; 34.5% of runners) ran at 88 +/- 6% CS, finished in 217.3 +/- 33.1 min and decoupled at 33.4 +/- 9.0 km; moderate (1.1 to <1.2; 32.7%) 86% CS, 224.9 min, 22.6 km; high (>=1.2; 32.8%) 82% CS, 238.5 min, 19.1 km (all p<0.01).
Males had greater decoupling than females (1.17 +/- 0.22 vs 1.12 +/- 0.16) and earlier onset (25.0 vs 26.3 km; both p<0.01).
Adding decoupling magnitude and onset to CS plus curvature-constant models reduced marathon prediction error from 6.45% to 5.16%.
limitations: Observational, marathon-only; decoupling is measured during the race itself, so it cannot be known in advance without an unvalidated long-run proxy; HR-based internal load is sensitive to heat, hydration and cardiac drift; groups differ in ability, so cause and effect are unclear.
implications: Compute a decoupling index (%HRmax per %CS, late segment over early segment) from long runs as a durability metric and use it to adjust marathon/ultra predictions (6.45% to 5.16% error in this dataset). Whether long-run decoupling matches race decoupling is untested.
Treat decoupling >=1.2 as a high-fade profile and lower the target fraction of CS (about 82% versus 88% in low-decoupling runners).
Use about 25 km as the average onset when scheduling long-run decoupling checks; the proxy needs back-testing.
Compute a per-run decoupling ratio: (HR as %HRmax divided by speed as %CS) in the late segment divided by the same in the 5-10 km segment; flag onset when the ratio exceeds 1.025.
Use bands low <1.1, moderate 1.1 to <1.2, high >=1.2 for race feedback; use ratio and onset as predictors in the marathon-time model (about 1.3 percentage points of error reduction in the paper).
Apply to hilly or hot races only after adjusting for terrain and temperature, which this analysis did not do.

verification.notes: Crossref and PubMed abstract re-fetched; the Europe PMC rendering truncated at '<', so PubMed was used to confirm thresholds (<1.1, >=1.1 to <1.2, >=1.2), onset definition and the 6.45% to 5.16% result. Added the moderate-group and sex-onset numbers.
